name: Declinism
statement: People report that other people are getting less kind and honest, while survey measures of how their contemporaries behave stay flat across the same decades.
meaning: Declinism is a belief about the world, not a memory of one's own life. The version that has been tested is narrow. Asked whether people in general have become less honest, kind or trustworthy, respondents say yes, in every decade and nearly every country where the question has been put. The case for calling that an illusion rests on a mismatch between two kinds of survey question. Items that ask people to compare now with then produce reports of decline. Items that ask people to report the behaviour they met in the past year produce flat lines. Neither kind of item measures morality directly, and no objective register of everyday kindness exists to check either against. The unit of the finding is the survey item and the population average, not the individual respondent.

origin.who: Richard P. Eibach, Lisa K. Libby and Thomas D. Gilovich
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper "When change in the self is mistaken for change in the world" reported that respondents' own life changes, such as becoming a parent or a change in finances, correlated with how much social change they perceived in things like crime rates. The authors proposed that misattributing self-change to world-change helps explain widespread beliefs in societal decline. It was read at abstract level only, so no sample sizes or coefficients from it are quoted here. The word "declinism" is older than the psychology and no academic source for its coinage was located; Feng, Wildschut, Sedikides and Dang define it in 2025 as the belief that things are gradually becoming worse.

evidence: Mastroianni and Gilbert assembled the survey record in 2023. They searched the Roper iPoll database and the archives of the General Social Survey, Pew, Gallup, the American National Election Studies, the World Values Survey and the European Social and Values Surveys. That turned up 177 items putting the question to 220,772 representative US respondents between 1949 and 2019. On 84.18% of those items a majority reported that morality had declined. The year of the survey did not predict that proportion, b = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.24], t(175) = 0.77, P = 0.45, with a Bayes factor of 0.04 against an effect. A second sweep found 58 items covering 354,120 people in 59 other nations between 1996 and 2007, and a majority reported decline on 86.21% of them. Respondents were not uniformly gloomy: 59% reported improved treatment of African Americans, 51% for people with physical disabilities and 50% for gay people. Their study 4 turned to items about present conduct, such as whether the respondent had been treated with respect yesterday or had let a stranger go ahead in a queue. Across 107 items put to 4,483,136 Americans between 1965 and 2020, the survey year explained under 0.3% of the variance on average, and under 0.2% across 33 non-US samples totalling 7,432,736 people. The whole paper covers 12,492,983 people. In their own study 2a, 698 Prolific respondents rated people as less kind, honest, nice and good in 2020 (M = 4.39) than in 2000 (M = 4.91), d = -0.71. Two mechanisms are proposed together as BEAM, biased exposure and biased memory: attention and media skew towards bad news about strangers, and negative memories fade faster, so the present looks worse than a past that has been quietly cleaned up. Two predictions followed. In study 5a, 283 respondents said people in general had declined between 2005 and 2020 (M = -0.36, d = 0.36) but that the individuals in their own personal world had improved (M = 0.23, t(255) = 4.86, d = 0.30). In study 5b, 387 respondents perceived decline after their own birth but none before it: ratings for the birth year and for 20 years earlier were equivalent (100% of the high-density interval inside the region of practical equivalence). Protzko and Schooler had already found the same shape in beliefs about the young. Across five preregistered studies with 3,458 American adults, respondents said children respect their elders less than they used to (b = 0.503, SE = 0.112, P < 0.001, n = 1,824) and enjoy reading less (b = 1.189, SE = 0.114, P < 0.001, n = 1,500). Which decline a person perceived tracked what that person was good at. Authoritarian respondents saw less respect, well-read respondents saw less reading, and more intelligent respondents saw falling intelligence. The crime version is visible in Gallup's own numbers. Frank Newport reports that in all but three of 32 measures taken since 1989, majorities of Americans have said crime nationally is increasing, which does not fit the recorded crime data. In the poll of 1 to 16 October 2025, 49% said there was more crime in the United States than a year earlier, against 30% who said so of their own area. On seriousness the gap was wider: 49% called national crime extremely or very serious against 12% for local crime.

replication.headline: An independent group repeated study 5b with 533 participants in 2024 and all four of its primary findings held.
replication.detail: Transparent Replications by Clearer Thinking ran study 5b again with 533 participants after exclusions, aged 18 to 69 and stratified across ten age groups. Perceived decline from birth to the present held, t = -13.915, P < 0.001, as did decline from the birth year to twenty years later, t = -6.015, P < 0.001. The two comparisons covering years before the participant was born came out equivalent, P = 0.485 and P = 0.034. The report gave the original paper five stars for replicability and 4.25 for transparency, marking it down because study 5b was not preregistered. Mastroianni and Gilbert also report two direct repeats of their own study 2a, one of them preregistered, with the same results. What has been repeated is the perception, not the archival argument. No independent redoing of study 4, the analysis that carries the claim that nothing has actually declined, was located.

study.cite: Transparent Replications by Clearer Thinking (2024). Report #10: Replication of a study from "The illusion of moral decline" (Nature | Mastroianni & Gilbert 2023).

limits: The strong claim is that morality has not declined, and the evidence for it is subjective. Mastroianni and Gilbert say so themselves, writing that their measures "are not definitive" while arguing that the wording of items about queues and strangers is too concrete to have drifted in meaning. The one objective figure they offer, a rise in prisoner's dilemma cooperation between 1956 and 2017, is credited to Yuan and colleagues and is quoted here from their description of it rather than from that paper. Their original studies used only US samples, and the non-US archival items span 13 years, from 1996 to 2007, against 70 for the US series. Decline is not the default belief about everything. Hillman, Antoun and Hauser report five studies of an improvement default, in which people presume things have got better in domains they know nothing about, including historical periods that in fact declined. Beliefs about the young are also domain-specific rather than global. Protzko and Schooler found that the average American did not think children were less intelligent than in the past, P > 0.81, even though the belief appeared for respect and reading. Eibach, Libby and Gilovich (2003) was read at abstract level only and no figures from it appear above. No peer-reviewed rebuttal of the 2023 paper was found in a search of the 49 works OpenAlex records as citing it, or in web searches for published comment; the critiques located were blog posts and are not cited here.
misreadings: Declinism is not rosy retrospection, and the two are routinely merged. Rosy retrospection compares one person's later rating of an event against the rating they gave while it was happening. Declinism is a judgement about other people across historical time. They come apart in the data. In Mastroianni and Gilbert's study 5a the same respondents said people in general had got worse while the people they personally knew had got better. The second error is a unit error. The figure 84.18% is the share of survey items on which a majority reported decline, not the share of people who believe in decline. The third is treating it as a political marking. More conservative respondents perceived more decline, but liberal respondents perceived decline too, M = -0.35, t(398) = -4.96, P < 0.001, d = 0.28 in study 2a. Protzko and Schooler found political conservatism unrelated to the belief that children no longer enjoy reading, P > 0.25. Older people are not more prone to it in the way the stereotype suggests. Older respondents reported more total decline, and study 2c showed this was because they were reporting across more years: the perceived annual rate did not differ by age, b = -0.0002, 95% CI [-0.0005, 0.0002], P = 0.29. The last error is reading the illusion as settled for every domain. It is a claim about aggregate perception across survey items, and where objective series exist, as with recorded crime, the mismatch has to be shown against those series rather than assumed.
